articles.headline: Mega Millions moved to a 24-ball Mega Ball pool on April 8, 2025
articles.description: On April 8, 2025, Mega Millions changed its matrix from 5-of-70 plus a Mega Ball of 25 to 5-of-70 plus a Mega Ball of 24. Draws before and after that date are read against different formats, which matters when you check older tickets or browse archives.
articles.bottomLine: Bottom Line: Since the drawing of April 8, 2025, Mega Millions has drawn its Mega Ball from a pool of 24 instead of 25. The five main numbers still come from a pool of 70, and results before that date must be read against the older format.
articles.beforeAfterLabel: Mega Millions matrix, before and after April 8, 2025
body: Mega Millions changed its drawing matrix with the drawing of April 8, 2025. The five main numbers are still drawn from a pool of 70, and the Mega Ball is now drawn from a pool of 24 rather than 25.

The format it replaced had been in effect since October 31, 2017: five main numbers from 70 and a Mega Ball from 25, with a separate Megaplier structure. LotteryCorner's result-format records model both eras as date-bounded formats, so a drawing is always read against the rules that were in force on its draw date.

For players, the practical effect is about reading results correctly. A ticket or an archived result from March 2025 belongs to the older format; one from May 2025 belongs to the current one. LotteryCorner's result pages apply the format that matches each drawing's date, so historical results keep their original meaning.

The change is recorded in LotteryCorner's production-derived format definitions, which carry the effective dates for both eras. Anything this article does not state — prices, odds or prize structures — is outside what those records evidence, and we do not guess at it.

articles.headline: Powerball's current 69/26 matrix took effect on October 7, 2015
articles.description: Powerball has drawn five main numbers from a pool of 69 and a Powerball from a pool of 26 since the drawing of October 7, 2015. Earlier drawings used different number ranges, so archived results are read against the format in force on their draw date.
articles.bottomLine: Bottom Line: Every Powerball drawing since October 7, 2015 uses five main numbers from a pool of 69 and a Powerball from a pool of 26. Drawings before that date used different ranges, and LotteryCorner reads each result against the format that was in force when it was drawn.
body: The Powerball format in use now — five main numbers drawn from a pool of 69 and a Powerball drawn from a pool of 26 — took effect with the drawing of October 7, 2015.

Drawings before that date used different main-number and Powerball ranges. LotteryCorner's result-format records model the boundary as an effective date, so a 2014 drawing and a 2016 drawing are each read against their own era's rules rather than against a single current format.

This matters most in the archives. A results page that applied the current 69/26 ranges to a pre-2015 drawing would describe numbers that could never have been drawn together under the old rules. Date-bounded formats are how historical result display stays correct.

Our records document the current era's ranges and its start date. The precise ranges of earlier eras are noted in the records as different but are not fully enumerated there, so this article does not state them — where evidence stops, so does the story.

articles.headline: How yearly results archives work on LotteryCorner
articles.description: A guide to LotteryCorner's yearly results archives: how drawings are grouped by the game's own local draw date, why a year page shows every drawing from that calendar year, and how to move between a game page and its history.
articles.bottomLine: Bottom Line: A yearly archive collects every drawing a game held in one calendar year, grouped by the game's own local draw date. It is the fastest way to check an old ticket or follow how a game's results ran across a season.
body: A yearly results archive is one game's drawings for one calendar year, in one place. Where a game page answers "what was drawn most recently", the archive answers "what was drawn on a date I have in mind".

Dates in an archive follow the game's own local draw date. A drawing that happened late in the evening belongs to the day it was drawn where the game is played — not to the next day in some other timezone. That rule keeps a ticket's printed date and the archive's date in agreement.

Archives are organised by year because that is how people remember tickets: a drawing from last spring, a ticket found in a winter coat. Opening the game's page and stepping into the right year is usually faster than scrolling a long feed.

Formats can change between years. When a game changes its number ranges, the archive keeps each drawing under the rules that were in force on its draw date, so older results always mean what they meant when they were published.

articles.headline: Ball groups, special balls and multipliers: what a result format is
articles.description: An explainer of the parts of a lottery result: main-number groups, named special balls like the Powerball and Mega Ball, and multipliers. Knowing the parts makes any game's results page easier to read.
articles.bottomLine: Bottom Line: Every lottery result is built from a few reusable parts — one or more groups of main numbers, sometimes a named special ball drawn from its own pool, and sometimes a multiplier. Once you can name the parts, any results page reads the same way.
body: Start with the main numbers. Most draw games pick a fixed count of numbers from one pool — five from 69 in Powerball, five from 70 in Mega Millions, three digits from 0–9 in a Pick 3. That set is the result's first ball group.

Some games add a special ball drawn from its own separate pool, with its own name: the Powerball, the Mega Ball, a Cash Ball or a Bonus ball. Because it comes from a separate pool, the special ball can repeat a main number — that is normal, not a misprint.
Multipliers such as Power Play sit beside the drawn numbers rather than among them. They scale certain prizes and are shown as part of the result, but they are not a ball from the main pools.

Formats also change over time, which is why LotteryCorner models them with effective dates. A results page that knows a game's format for each era can render any drawing — recent or historical — with the right groups, the right pools and the right labels.
